did_you_know.text: Did you know? Chapter 31 opens with the words of King Lemuel and with the "oracle"—advice or instruction—that his mother taught him.
Did you know? Lemuel’s mother warns him not to give his strength to desires that could weaken his leadership, especially relationships and actions that could lead to the ruin of kings.
Did you know? Kings and rulers are commanded to avoid wine and strong drink, so that they do not drink, forget the law, or distort justice for the poor.
Did you know? Lemuel is urged to speak up for the mute and for everyone who cannot defend themselves or plead their own case.
Did you know? The woman of noble character is described as rare and precious, worth far more than jewels.
Did you know? One sign of a woman of noble character is the trust her husband places in her; the passage emphasizes that he lacks nothing of value because of her.
Did you know? The woman of noble character is not content with household work alone: she considers buying a field, purchases it with the fruit of her labor, and plants a vineyard.
Did you know? The woman of noble character combines diligence with generosity: she opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy.
Did you know? The woman of noble character plans ahead for her family’s needs in the cold season, so she is not afraid of snow; everyone in her household is dressed in warm clothing.

Did you know? At the end of the poem, it is emphasized that beauty and charm are fleeting, while a woman who fears the Lord is worthy of praise; therefore, her deeds and the fruits of her labor are praised at the city gates.
